paragraphs.text: This essay looks at GPT-3, a huge program OpenAI released in May 2020 that learned by predicting the next word in Internet text. It was 117 times larger than GPT-2, the model before it. It showed "meta-learning": learning how to learn, so it picked up new tasks from just a few examples.

paragraphs.text: The author says this supports the "scaling hypothesis": that intelligence may come mainly from simple learning parts run at enormous size. If so, these systems will keep getting smarter as computing power grows. GPT-3 was costly for AI research but cheap by government or business budgets, so far bigger models are possible.

paragraphs.text: A key idea is the "blessings of scale": bigger models trained on more data tend to learn better and more general skills. GPT-3's gains kept following the predicted curve, with no sign of leveling off. The author also argues that predicting text nearly perfectly requires real understanding, so the last, hardest gains matter most.

fuller.text: This essay asks what GPT-3 tells us about the future of AI. GPT-3 is a huge program from OpenAI, released in May 2020, that learned by predicting the next word in Internet text. The author defends the "scaling hypothesis": the idea that intelligence may come from simple learning methods made very large, with lots of data and computing power.

The author defends the "scaling hypothesis": the idea that intelligence may come from simple learning methods made very large, with lots of data and computing power.

fuller.text: GPT-3 was over ten times bigger than any earlier network, yet its gains did not level off as many expected. It also showed meta-learning: learning a new task from a few examples, though nobody built it to do that. The author says this means far bigger models are both possible and useful, at costs small by government or business standards.

fuller.text: A key idea is the "blessings of scale": bigger networks often learn faster, more stably and more generally. The author's guess is that a big network holds countless small sub-models, and enough hard data pushes out lazy shortcuts like memorizing. He also argues that the last, hardest bits of prediction error need real reasoning, so better prediction may demand real understanding.

brief.text: This essay looks at GPT-3, a huge computer program trained to guess the next word in text from the internet. The author uses it to argue for the "scaling hypothesis": the idea that simple learning programs grow smarter just by being made bigger. That means more size, more data, and more computing power.
